opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
This line comes from the parable of The Rich Man and Lazarus.
“Moreover, between us and you a great chasm is established…”
It is one of the most unsettling lines Jesus speaks about the reality of judgment. The rich man can see Lazarus. He can see Abraham. He can even speak to them. But he cannot reach them. The separation is fixed. The distance cannot be crossed.
What is striking is that the chasm did not suddenly appear in eternity. It had already been forming during the man’s life.
The rich man lived comfortably. Lazarus lay at his gate. Day after day, the man passed him. Hunger, sores, humiliation—right outside his door. And yet the rich man remained untouched by it, with utter indifference. A life so absorbed in itself that it never bent down to see the person at the threshold.
So when Abraham says a great chasm has been established, it is not arbitrary. It is the final shape of a life that never crossed the small distances God placed right in front of it.
The man who would not cross the few feet to Lazarus now finds himself unable to cross the infinite distance to mercy.
That is what makes the parable so pleading. The chasm was not created by geography. It was created by the habits of the heart.
And even in torment, the rich man still speaks the same way: “Send Lazarus.” As if Lazarus were still there to serve him. The man sees him, but he still does not truly see him.
Jesus is exposing something deeper than wealth or poverty. He is exposing the quiet ways people move past one another—climbing over each other, overlooking each other, stepping around each other—pursuing position, comfort, success, importance.
All the while, the kingdom of God is unfolding in the opposite direction.
Not upward. Toward one another.
Toward the small crossings that close distance between people: a hand extended, a door opened, a table shared, a ride given, a burden lifted.
These are the bridges of the Kingdom.
And Jesus is warning us gently but clearly: the distances we refuse to cross now have a way of becoming the distances we cannot cross later.
